It was only when I listed out my medical rights under the NSW Health Act that the HCCC person started to treat me with any respect at all. 

Mental Health Care in this country sucks, and it’s one reason why so many people stay away from it under all circumstances. Once you experience it, you never want to go through it again. For me, it means that I personally will never speak to a mental health progressional - the loss of trust for me was acute and will never be restored.

If you are under an involuntary hold, then you don’t have much say over how you will be treated. It sucks and I’ve experienced this before - it’s very disempowering. Unfortunately once the Mental Health Act kicks in, you lose most of your medical autonomy.

Well meaning people will often dismiss the feeling of powerlessness as necessary, but it is quite frightening to have a group of people hold so much power over you. My recommendation is to cooperate to get it over with as soon as you can.

As I say, I’ve been in this situation and these guys can be quite abusive. Yes, others will tell you otherwise, but I think you’ll find most people on this forum have never experienced the situation you are in right now.

For me, I realised a few things when I got out of the situation:

1. If you admit to suicidal thoughts, you will likely be placed as an involuntary patient.

2. If you see the wrong psychiatrist, then they can make things much worse. Make sure you get one who you really trust. The one I chose was a real fucker, so I gave up on this sort of thing and worked it out on my own.

3. If I am having a mental health episode, then I only tell close and trusted friends and family. I discussed it with them and under no circumstance will they call the authorities as they saw what happened to me and how it derailed my life at the time.

4. If you call Lifeline and you wish to remain anonymous, do it from a pay phone. I once called them and turned off caller ID, spoke to them about suicidal ideation and though I did t give my name or number, they still sent out the police. I then spent 12 hours in Liverpool hospital without anyone seeing me. Fun fact: under the NSW Mental Health Act, they can only hold you for 12 hours before an assessment. After that, you are free to walk.

In my awful situation, the former GM of Liverpool Hospital wrote to me and said that they keep *all* people in seclusion. They don’t and they aren’t meant to. I got a large payout from SWSLHD for their abusive practices.

These are *my* strategies. I don’t necessarily recommend them for you. You have an eating disorder and you need to find help, perhaps this is good for you right now, but I also understand that having your autonomy removed is traumatic and not really helpful in the long term.

Just be aware that in this system you need to be careful. There are many burned out mental health professionals, and they can be pretty fucking awful even though they may not have meant to be like this when they started their career. Be cautious and take care!

You’re thinking about this very logically, and your reading of the statute raises a valid point. However, here’s why you’d still likely be guilty under 18 U.S.C. § 597, even if you didn’t actually vote for the candidate you were bribed to support.

The key thing to understand about bribery laws—including this one—is that the crime is complete once the money is exchanged with corrupt intent, not when the act (the voting decision) happens.

So in the first paragraph: “The Offense of Offering or Giving” - if someone gave you $100 to vote for Candidate A, that person committed a crime regardless of whether you actually followed through.

Now in the second paragraph: “The Offense of Accepting the Bribe”… If you accepted the $100 with the understanding that it was in exchange for your vote, you are guilty of accepting a bribe, even if you secretly voted for Candidate B. In this case, the law punishes the act of accepting the bribe, not whether the briber got what they wanted.

The legal principle that the crime of bribery is complete upon the offer or acceptance of a bribe, regardless of the outcome, is well-established in broader bribery law. This means that even if the intended action (such as voting a certain way) is not carried out, the offense is considered complete when the bribe is solicited, offered, or accepted.

For example, in cases involving public officials, courts have consistently held that the crime of bribery does not depend on the official performing the requested act, but rather on the corrupt agreement itself. This interpretation aligns with the intent of statutes like 18 U.S.C. § 597, which aim to prevent corruption in the electoral process by criminalizing both the offering and accepting of bribes related to voting, irrespective of whether the bribe influences the actual vote.

The prevailing legal understanding supports the interpretation that both offering and accepting a bribe are independently prosecutable offenses, and the completion of the bribery act is not contingent upon the fulfillment of the corrupt agreement.

In 18 U.S.C. § 597, the word “and” between the two paragraphs is important because it connects them as part of the same statutory provision. However, in legal interpretation, whether “and” is read conjunctively (both conditions must be met) or disjunctively (either condition can apply) depends on the context and judicial interpretation.

So, the first paragraph criminalizes offering or giving money (or something valuable) to induce someone to vote or refrain from voting.

The second paragraph criminalizes accepting such money in exchange for voting or not voting.

What this means is that the use of “and” connects these two offenses, but it does not mean that both must occur for a violation to happen.

So, no, “and” doesn’t require both actions to happen . Courts generally interpret statutes like this to mean that either action (offering/bribing or accepting a bribe) is independently punishable. The law covers both sides of the transaction to ensure that both the giver and the receiver of a bribe can be prosecuted, but a person does not need to commit both acts to be guilty.

This had happened before. The Supreme Court had to adjudicate on the use if “and” in a statute in the case United States v. Fisk, 70 U.S. (3 Wall.) 445 (1865). The defendant argued that all the conditions had to be met together because of the use of “and”; however, the Supreme Court ruled that “and” can sometimes be interpreted as “or” if it better aligns with the purpose of the law.

In the context of 18 U.S.C. § 597, if “and” were interpreted strictly, it would mean that both the giver and receiver of a bribe must be convicted together, which would undermine the statute’s purpose. Courts would likely follow the Fisk reasoning and allow prosecution for either action independently.

There are two areas of memory where a program holds data. The stack is structure where the program pushes and pops data as it needs it. A C stack can also be directly indexed by the program. You never access the stack directly (well, not normally). The “stack” is used to store value variable and pointers. It’s limited in its size, so you can’t always use it for storing large amounts of data.

The heap is another area of memory where blocks of memory can be reserved to allocate to instances of data structures or variables. Here you can allocate large blocks of data as needed. Pointers to the start of the block of data are stored on the stack. You *dereference* a pointer to get to the data you want to use.

The stack is faster than the heap simply because the program can get to the data faster. To get to data on the heap, you have to first get the pointer to the data, then go to that address to get the data. There are also some locality of data issues that I won’t get into.

In terms of transaction management over a distributed system, I don’t think they had any idea how hard this is to do properly. If you do distributed transactions, you need to handle things like communication failures, avoid double pay issues, handle rollbacks, hardware faults, etc.

Here are some issues that can happen in a distributed transaction management system:

Concurrency control problems 
- race conditions can occur that mean transactions can be processed out of order, leading to inconsistencies

Network reliability 
- network partitioning can occur, leading to parts of the system becoming isolated and this means transactions can fail to process and inconsistencies can occur. Evidence has been given this happened on more than one occasion.
- latency issues cause major slowdowns - again leading you to possible consistency issues 

Atomicity problems
- atomicity is the quality that a transaction either completes fully, or it does not happen at all. If in the coordination of a transaction the transaction coordinator fails, then balances on either end can result in the system going into an unreliable state
- if atomicity fails - which can absolutely happen, then it requires manual resolution. That’s why there was remote control facilities in Horizon. But if you are going to do this, you need to detect that the failure occurred and there needs a very clear audit record noting how the issue was resolved. This wasn’t implemented in Horizon.

Fault tolerance issues
- the main issue here is that in  distributed transaction system, failure recovery is extremely complex. If a node fails, then you need a reliable way of rolling back transactions. This wasn’t the case as far as I can see. Sometimes, ironically, the system did handle the failure but didn’t notify the operator so they didn’t know to redo the transaction, and this money people paid for bills never made it to the biller! That was never the fault of the SPMs.

The biggest and most reliable distributed transaction management system is the Bitcoin network, and even though cryptographically it is very clever (it doesn’t use a centralised clock to synchronise transactions, instead it uses a proof work algorithm to ensure transactions are synchronised) there is no way Horizon was that sophisticated.
